Gaṇeśasūkta
------------------------------------------
Some sūktas, of the ऋग्वेद have been designated as ‘Abhiṣeka-sūktas’ since they are used for अभिषेक or bathing the images in ritualistic worship. This Gaṇeśa-sūkta is one of them.
Though it has been called Gaṇeśa-sūkta it has nothing to do with the गणेश or गणपति of paurāṇic fame.
It consists of 12 mantras, out of which the first nine are from the 81st सूक्त of the 8th मण्डल (8.81.1-9). The tenth is Ṛgveda (2.23.1) and the last two are Ṛgveda (10.112.9 and 10).
Kusīdī-Kāṇva is the ṛṣi or the sage for the first nine mantras. इन्द्र is the devatā or deity. For the tenth मन्त्र गृत्समद is the sage and बृहस्पति/ ब्रह्मणस्पति are the deities. And, for the last two, Nabhaḥprabhedana is the sage and इन्द्र is the deity.
A brief summary of the mantras is as follows:
O इन्द्र! You have a liberal hand (i.e., large-hearted). You please hold (in that [right] hand) the wealth which is excellent and attractive, so that you can grant it to us.
इन्द्र, we know that you have accomplished many great deeds, that you are a bestower of many gifts, that you are the lord of immense wealth, that you are of immense size and a great protector.
O hero इन्द्र! When you decide to bestow (gifts or wealth), none, neither the gods nor human beings, can thwart you even as a powerful bull cannot be thwarted.
(O men of the world!) Come here quickly. Let us praise इन्द्र, the lord who is self-resplendent. Let none who is arrogant due to wealth, harm us!
May इन्द्र praise or sing hymns along with us. May he listen to our songs of praise (sāma). May he accept us, who are endowed with wealth.
Indra! Bring and distribute wealth to us with both your hands. Do not sever us from wealth.
O destroyer of enemies! Approach the wealth of the miser and bring it to us with your power.
Indra! the wise ones have deposited ड़ोओद् (or wealth) with you. Being requested by us, grant it to us abundantly.
Men, full of desires, are praising you. May the food—(objects of desire) which are pleasing to all—come to us quickly.
Brahmaṇaspati! You are the chief leader of the heavenly bands. You are the best of sages. You abound in ड़ोओद्. You shine among those who deserve to be praised. You are the master of Vedic mantras. We invite you to our Vedic rituals. Sit down in our sacrificial shed, listen to our praises and protect us.
Indra, the lord of the groups (of the Maruts)! Be seated among those who are praying. They (who know you) declare that you are the wisest among those who are wise. Without you no rite can be performed whether near or far off. O lord of wealth! Venerate our hymns of praise which are great and variegated.
The Rich One! Make us—who are praying to you—bright and brilliant. You, the lord of wealth, are our friend. Understand our prayers. You, the warrior endowed with great strength, fight on our behalf. Give us a share in the undivided riches.

gaṇḍakāla
(‘inauspicious time’)
------------------------------------------
In Hindu अस्त्रोलोग्य्, the birth of a baby at certain times considered as inauspicious forebodes evil to its parents, One such inauspicious time is called ‘gaṇḍakāla’.
For instance, the first three ghaṭikās (1 ghaṭikā = 24 minutes) when the three nakṣatras अश्विनी, (the स्तर्स् beta and gamma, arietis), Makha (the स्तर्स् alpha, eta, gamma, zeta, mu and epsilon leonis) and Mūlā (the स्तर्स् lambda and upsilon scorpii) are present, are inauspicious. If it occurs in the night and the baby is born at that time it forebodes evil for the मोथेर्.

Gaṇḍabheruṇḍa
------------------------------------------
The गण्डभेरुण्ड, a doubleheaded eagle, has been the State symbol of many a royal dynasty, especially in South India. Prominent among them are the emperors of Vijayanagara and the kings of Mysore. It continues to be so, of the Karnataka State even now.
According to the highly sectarian accounts of the पुराणस्, विष्णु as नरसिṁह was conquered by शिव as शरभ (an animal more fierce than the lion). Then विष्णु took the form of गण्डभेरुण्ड and subdued शिव in the guise of शरभ!
The bird सुपर्ण of the Ṛgveda may be an early edition of this bird-monster.
The गण्डभेरुण्ड symbol has been traced to the इन्दुस् वल्लेय् चिविलिसतिओन्, at मोहेन्जो दारो and later found at तक्षशिला (Taxila) also.
The well-known folk-tale poem, the Pañcatantra, mentions this bird in one of its tales.
In the village Baḷḷigāve in the Shimoga district of Karnataka, there is a pillar of the Cāḷukyan era (A. D. 1047) depicting the deity Bheruṇḍeśvara (deified गण्डभेरुण्ड) along with an edict.
The bird—according to the archaeo-logists and historians—signifies peace, progress and power.

Gaṇapati Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
Gaṇapati or गणेश is an extremely popular deity in हिन्दुइस्म्. Three minor उपनिषद्स् deal with him, this being one of them. It belongs to the Atharvaveda.
Comprising 19 sections it is mostly in prose, interspersed here and there, with verses in the śloka metre.
The first two verses identify गणपति with ब्रह्मा, विष्णु, and महेश्वर, responsible for च्रेअतिओन्, preservation and destruction of this world. He is also ब्रह्मन् and आत्मन्.
He is ṛta and सत्य, the cosmic order and truth.
The fourth section prays to him for protection, not only of the teacher and the disciple but also of all things in all directions. Then only can we live here safely and happily.
The next verse identifies him with speech, चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् and bliss. In fact he is the ब्रह्मन्, the one without a second.
The sixth section describes him as responsible for च्रेअतिओन्, preservation and dissolution of the world. He is also identified with the five elements in the created world, like the earth and water. He is the four aspects of speech like parā and पश्यन्ती. He is beyond the three well-known guṇas, the three bodies, and the three aspects of time. He is the deity presiding over the मूलाधार centre. It is upon him that the yogis meditate.
The next three verses describe the गणपति मन्त्र. Gaṇaka is the sage who discovered the मन्त्र. ‘Gaṁ’ is the seed letter; and ‘gāṁ’ should be used for purposes of न्यास (purificatory process for the limbs of the body). The letter ‘laṁ’ must be used in the पूजा with five items. The मन्त्र itself is ‘Oṁ gaṇapataye namaḥ.’
The tenth verse contains the famous गणेश-गायत्री-मन्त्र:
ekadantāya vidmahe
vakratuṇḍāya dhīmahi
tanno dantiḥ pracodayāt ॥
‘We know him who has only one tusk. We meditate upon him with a bent trunk. May he, the Lord with tusks (i.e., गणपति), impel (us in the right direction, i.e., towards himself).’
The next four verses—11th to the 14th describe गणपति’s form and attri-butes to facilitate meditation:
He has one (unbroken) tusk and four hands, holding the noose and the goad in two, the other two exhibiting the poses of granting boons and protection. His complexion is red all over. He is wearing red dress and flowers. He is the origin of the universe. Yet, he is the all-merciful god, especially towards his votaries.
One who meditates on him thus, is the best of yogis.
Section sixteen describes the effects and fruits of knowing and realising this science related to गणपति. Freedom from sins and attaining the four ends of life (puruṣārthas) are the most prominent among them.
This spiritual wisdom must be taught only to a worthy disciple and never to others.
The last section describes the various ritualistic processes meant to be adopted by those who have specific desires to be fulfilled. Attaining oratory, scholarship, freedom from fear, obtaining fame, destruction of obstacles, gaining the power of a mantra—these are some of the things mentioned.
The Upaniṣad concludes with the statement that one becomes all knowing by a knowledge of this science.
See also GAṆAPATI and UPANIṢADS.

Gāṇapatyas
(‘those following the cult of गणपति’)
------------------------------------------
Gaṇapati has been one of the most popular and important of the deities of the Hindu pantheon. The गाणपत्यस् were members of a powerful sect that considered गणपति as the Supreme God. The sect might have originated during the seventh century A. D. It became powerful around the tenth century and declined later.
The Gaṇeśapurāṇa and the Gaṇeśagītā are the basic works accepted by this cult.
This cult envisages the worship of five kinds of गणपति along with their Śaktis or spouses. They are: उच्छिष्ट-गणपति, Mahā-गणपति, Ūrdhva-गणपति, Piṅgala-गणपति and लक्ष्मी-गणपति.
Out of these, worship of the first aspect clearly belongs to the वामाचार cults and is against the Vedic traditions.
Later on, the Gāṇāpatyas got divided into six separate sects.
Śaṅkara (A. D. 788-820) is said to have converted most members of the sect to Vedic practices.

Gaṇeśapurāṇa
------------------------------------------
The main purpose of the पुराणस् or mythological lore is to bring philosophy and religion to the doors of the masses. They have also played an important role in spreading knowledge—both sacred and secular—and preserve हिन्दु चुल्तुरे among the common people.
Out of the eighteen उपपुराणस् or secondary पुराणस्, (all ascribed to the sage व्यास), the Gaṇeśapurāṇa is listed as the first. It is a big work of 12,000 verses spread over 250 chapters. Except for the Gaṇeśagītā, an important treatise on religion and philosophy, which forms a part of the last portion of the purāṇa, the rest of the work is highly sectarian in character, clearly aimed at spreading the Gāṇapatya-cult (cult of गणपति). It abounds in stories of gods, sages and kings, always aimed at glorifying गणेश above even the well-known deities शिव, देवी, विष्णु and ब्रह्मा!
Incidentally, certain mantras of गणेश, vratas or religious observances and worship connected with him are also described.
See also GAṆEŚAGĪTĀ, PURĀṆAS and UPAPURĀṆAS.

Gaṇeśagītā
(‘the song of Lord गणेश’)
------------------------------------------
The Bhagavadgītā, a part and parcel of the immortal epic, the Mahābhārata, has left a very deep impression on the psyche of the Hindu nation. This has, in course of time, given rise to a number of similar works of a didactical nature, either as a part of some purāṇa or even as an independent work.
The Gaṇeśagītā is one typical example. It is an integral part of the Gaṇeśa-purāṇa, comprising the eleven chapters—138 to 148—and has 413 ślokas or verses in all. It is in the form of a dialogue between the king Vareṇya and his divine son Gajānana or गणेश.
Summary of the Contents
A brief summary of the work may now be attempted here.
Chapter 1
Sāṅkhyārthasārayoga, 69 verses
The king Vareṇya requests his son Gajānana (knowing full well that he is God himself) to expound to him yogaśāstra or the science of योग.
In reply, Gajānana discounts several concepts normally thought of as योग and states that true योग is withdrawing one’s मिन्द् from the objects of senses and directing it towards the आत्मन् within. In this attempt several modes of sādhanā like the साधनचतुष्टय, śravaṇa (hearing about the आत्मन्), मनन (reflection of the same) and निदिध्यासन (meditation), which are useful, are described. The need for a proper गुरु or spiritual teacher is also stressed.
Chapter 2
Karmayoga, 43 verses
In reply to the question whether jñānaniṣṭhā (devotion to knowledge) or karmaniṣṭhā (devotion to work) is a better path of sādhanā, Gajānana replies that both are equally effective if properly understood and practised. Work done as a duty and without selfish motives is far better than giving up work altogether. When प्रजापति created this world along with gods and men, as also the system of the four varṇas among men, he ordained that all should perform their duties and sustain one another by helping one another. Gajānana specifically declares that even the liberated ones should work to set an example to the ignorant people, of the world. Towards the end, in reply to another question, he says that it is काम or desire that impels a man to commit sins and hence exhorts Vareṇya to control it.
Chapter 3
Jñānapratipādanayoga, 50 verses
Continuing his teaching, Gajānana declares that he taught this ancient योग or spiritual wisdom to विष्णु in the beginning of च्रेअतिओन्. Through him and a succession of teachers like सूर्य and मनु it was propagated in this world. To the question how he, of this generation, could teach it to विष्णु, the ancient divine person, Gajānana reveals that he is the anādi-ईश्वर, the primeval Lord of the universe, who is the origin, the sustenance and the place of dissolution of the whole universe, from whom even विष्णु and other gods originate!
The ignorant persons worship other deities for petty results and hence are caught in the web of सṁसार or transmi-gration.
Gajānana declares that the system of the four varṇas was evolved by him. He also explains the terms kriyā (actions done without selfish desires) and akriyā (abandonment of prescribed actions), various yajñas, the importance of approaching a worthy गुरु and satsaṅga (holy company).
Chapter 4
Dvaidhasaṁnyāsayoga, 37 verses
Now, the king Vareṇya raises the question whether कर्मयोग or कर्म-सṁन्यास is superior. Though both are good and give the same result, Gajānana opines, that the former is better.
A true karmayogi offers the fruits of all his karmas to God. Hence he is not bound. It is the person who performs desire-motivated actions that is bound and hence suffers.
God never creates कर्म (action) or कर्तृत्व (agency). They are done by the प्रकृति of three guṇas. Those wise ones who know this are the real paṇḍitas (men of knowledge) and can get whatever they want.
In reply to another question, Gajānana describes the nature of true sukha or happiness, as the one rooted in the आत्मन् (Self).
Chapter 5
Yogāvṛttipraśaṁsanāyoga, 27 verses
Gajānana stresses that योग is possible only when the मिन्द् is purified by the performance of ordained works, but without the desire for the fruits. Such a work is called ‘akarma’. But, when work is performed with selfish motives and desires, it binds.
The divine teacher then describes in detail, the factors that are not conducive to the practice of योग like physical diseases, disturbed state of मिन्द्, unclean and risky places, very hot or cold seasons and so on. The practitioner of योग should also avoid going to extremes in the case of ड़ोओद्, ड़स्तिन्ग्, sleep or keeping awake.
Renunciation of desires is another important aspect of sādhanā.
In answer to two more questions raised by Vareṇya, the lord replies that the मिन्द्, though difficult to control can be brought round through वैराग्य (spirit of renunciation) and अभ्यास (repeated effort). If a योगि dies before reaching the final goal of life, he will be reborn in the family of yogis, after first enjoying divine pleasures in हेअवेन्. He will then continue his spiritual practices.
Chapter 6
Buddhiyoga, 21 verses
This chapter starts with a description of the twofold प्रकृति of the Lord—the lower प्रकृति comprising ten parts (four elements, मिन्द्, the sun and the मोओन् and three other aspects); the higher प्रकृति, viz., the जीव or cetana who is in the grip of अहङ्कार, born out of the attachment to the मिन्द्. The whole world is a product of these two prakṛtis.
People in general are overcome by प्रकृति and hence bound. However, once in a while, some fortunate सोउल्, purified through the performance of his ordained duties (varṇa-आश्रम-धर्म) crosses over this प्रकृति or māyā.
After describing how he is present in every object of the created world, Gajānana declares that even those who worship other gods with desires actually worship him alone. And again, it is he that responds to their supplications through them.
The importance of the final thoughts at the time of death is stressed at the end.
Chapter 7
Upāsanāyoga, 25 verses
This chapter begins with a short account of the two well-known paths described in the Upaniṣads—the देवयान or arcirādimārga and पितृयान or dhūmādi-mārga. They are the paths leading to the ब्रह्मलोक (the world of ब्रह्मा, the creator) and to the पितृलोक (the world of manes).
Brahman, the Absolute, is beyond both. It is identical with Gajānana himself. Those who meditate upon him attain this ब्रह्मन् and get मुक्ति or लिबेरतिओन्.
This meditation is aided by ritualistic worship performed with faith. And, this ritualistic worship can be performed mentally also.
Though sakāmapūjā (worship motivated by desires) is permissible, niṣkāma-पूजा (unselfish worship) is more desirable.
Since all the gods are the manifestations of the one God (Gajānana), it is not proper to dislike other gods even while being devoted to one of them.
A simple mode of mantrajapa (repetition of the divine name) along with its subsidiary processes like the nyāsas, is also described.
Towards the end, there is a eulogy of the प्रणव or ओङ्कार.
Chapter 8
Viśvarūpadarśanayoga, 25 verses
At the specific request of the king Vareṇya, Lord Gajānana shows him the cosmic form of his, after endowing him with a divine sight. Seeing that cosmic form, Vareṇya describes it and also praises the Lord. At his entreaties, the Lord withdraws the cosmic figure and re-assumes his original form. The description, though brief, is very similar to the one given in the Bhagavadgītā.
Chapter 9
Kṣetra-jñātṛ-jñeya-विवेक-yoga, 41 verses
Worshipping God with form and contemplating on the अक्षर/Avyakta (God, the formless) are two well-known modes of spiritual discipline. Which one is the better of the two? In reply to this question, Gajānana replies that both are equally effective. However, the former is easier whereas the latter is extremely hard.
In spiritual life, devotion is everything. Even the well-known sages like सनक, शुक or नारद became great because of भक्ति or devotion. Hence, meditating on the Lord, with steady devotion, results in योग and through that, attaining him.
Performance of one’s स्वधर्म or ordained duties and offering its fruits to the Lord, purifies the मिन्द्. Equanimity of मिन्द् too is a great help.
Then comes a description of the क्षेत्र and the क्षेत्रज्ञ. क्षेत्र is the physical body as well as the subtle body (the सूक्ष्मशरीर comprising 16 items) (and the jīvas too) whereas God is the क्षेत्रज्ञ residing in them all.
Jñāna or knowledge comprises several items of discipline such as ārjava (straight-forwardness), guruśuśrūṣā (ser-vice to the गुरु), virakti (detachment), equanimity, self-control and so on. This ज्ञान will ultimately help in the revelation of ब्रह्मन्, the Absolute.
This is then followed by a nice description of this ब्रह्मन् which again, is identified with Gaṇeśvara or Gajānana himself.
Chapter 10
Yogopadeśayoga, 23 verses
This chapter starts with a description of three kinds of prakṛti—sattva, रजस् and tamas—and the way they manifest in the human beings.
Sattva frees a person from the bondage of सṁसार whereas रजस् and तमस् bind him all the more.
The signs of सत्त्व, of daivī type, are: abhaya (fearlessness), अहिṁसा (non-injury to others), शौच (purity), apaiśunya (absence of calumny), amānitā (absence of pride and vanity) and so on.
The characteristics of a person of the āsurī type, of रजस्, are: bragging, arrogance, perverted understanding, short-temper, jealousy and so on.
The qualities seen in a person of the rākṣasī type, of तमस्, are: delusion, egoism, vanity, hatred, violence, anger, harming others for nothing, agnosticism, falsehood and many other evil qualities.
Whereas good persons go to हेअवेन् after death, the evil-doers go to हेल्ल्. But both of them come back to this earth again.
Even भक्ति or devotion can be of three types according to these guṇas. But devotees are always advised to cultivate sāttvic devotion only.
Chapter 11
Trividhavastunirūpaṇayoga, 52 verses
In this final chapter, there is a beautiful delineation of three kinds of तपस् (austerity), दान (gifts), ज्ञान (knowledge), कर्म (action), kartā (doer), sukha (happiness) and दुःख (unhappiness), according to the three guṇas of सत्त्व, रजस् and तमस्.
Serving the respected elders, perfor-mance of one’s ordained duties and worship of gods is तपस् of the body. Truthful and sweet speech is तपस् of speech. Keeping the मिन्द् unexcited and at peace is तपस् of the मिन्द्.
When this तपस् is performed without any desires, it is sāttvika. When done with desires it is rājasika, when practised to harm others or as a show, it is tāmasika.
Dāna or gifts when given as per the injunctions of the scriptures to the right person at the right time and place, is sāttvika. When given with selfish motives it is rājasika. If given to those who will dishonour or misuse it, it is tāmasika.
Similarly there is the three fold distinction in ज्ञान (knowledge) also. Seeing the Saccidānanda ब्रह्मन् everywhere is sāttvika ज्ञान. Seeing the limited jīvātman is rājasika ज्ञान. Mistaking the body for the आत्मन् is tāmasika ज्ञान.
Sāttvika karmas are the actions ordained by the scriptures, performed without selfish motives and in a way that does not inconvenience others. Rājasika karmas are performed as a show without the proper attitude. Foolish and idiotic actions are tāmasika.
A sāttvika kartā or doer, though he does actions rightly, is never egoistic. The rājasika doer is selfish and is subject to constantly changing moods. The tāmasika doer is always engaged in harming others.
Sāttvika sukha or happiness appears to cause difficulty in the beginning (because of the disciplines involved in attaining it) but gives bliss at the end. Happiness derived from sense-pleasures results in suffering at the end and hence is rājasika. The tāmasika happiness produces delusion and harm.
Then follows a brief explanation of a famous phrase Oṁ tat sat. A detailed account of the four varṇas—brāhmaṇas, kṣattriyas, vaiśyas and śūdras—and their duties is given next.
Towards the end there is the specific injunction that this teaching should not be imparted to the unworthy ones but to be protected by all means.
The teaching ends with a detailed phalaśruti or eulogy. There is also the instruction regarding the proper mode of reciting it including the recommendation of certain holy days and holy places.
Conclusion
A careful perusal of this Gaṇeśagītā reveals that it is almost an imitation, nay, an अदोप्तिओन्, of the celebrated Bhagavad-gītā. The topics discussed, the questions raised, the replies given are all very much reminiscent of the Gītā. The language is elegant and the presentation good. (It is said that there is a Sanskrit commentary too on this work. But not much is known about it.) In some places, it is even more detailed. On the whole, it is a work that deserves a deeper study.
See also GAṆEŚA-PURĀṆA.

gaṇḍānta
------------------------------------------
Belief in अस्त्रोलोग्य्, the effect of the movement of the heavenly bodies like the प्लनेत्स् and the स्तर्स् on human life, is a common phenomenon seen among all the people of the world. The word ‘gaṇḍānta’ used in Hindu अस्त्रोलोग्य्, is a technical word indicating certain inauspicious timings and combinations. They exert inauspicious influences on birth, मर्रिअगे, starting on a journey or an invasion and other similar incidents in life. For instance, the conjunction of the 15th tithi with pratipad for two ghaṭikās (48 minutes), the conjunction of Karkāṭaka (Cancer) and Siṁha (Leo) for half a ghaṭikā (12 minutes) or the conjunction of the स्तर्स् Revatī and अश्विनी for four ghaṭikās (96 minutes) are all गण्डान्त. These gaṇḍāntas produce evil effects on the child’s ड़थेर् or मोथेर् and so on. Hence all auspicious undertakings should be avoided during these periods.

Gāṇḍīva
(‘[a bow] made of the hide of a rhinoceros’)
------------------------------------------
The greatest archers found in the Hindu mythological literature are Śrī राम and अर्जुन. If Śrī राम’s bow was known as the Kodaṇḍa, अर्जुन’s was called the गाण्डीव.
This bow was made by ब्रह्मा (the four faced creator) himself with the hide of a Gaṇḍa or rhinoceros. (Hence the name गाण्डीव.) It was handed down to a succession of heroes as follows: प्रजापति, इन्द्र, चन्द्र and वरुण.
When अग्नि, the fire-god, wanted to devour the Khāṇḍava forest, वरुण lent the गाण्डीव bow to अर्जुन so that he could protect अग्नि. अर्जुन kept it for 65 years, fought all his battles with it, including the कुरुक्षेत्र war.
This bow was so versatile and powerful that one could fight with one lakh persons at a time!
Agni took it back for वरुण when अर्जुन was on his last journey (mahā prasthāna).

Gaṇḍakī
(‘that [which has flown] from the cheeks’)
------------------------------------------
Gaṇḍakī is the same as the modern river Gaṇḍak. It gets its name from the fact—as per the accounts given in the Varāhapurāṇa (ch. 144)—that it was formed from the sweat on the cheeks of Mahāviṣṇu (gaṇḍa = cheek). Other names are Śālagrāmī, Saptagaṇḍakī and नारायणी.
It rises in the हिमालयस्, passes through Nepal and joins the river गङ्गा at Sonepur in the Muzaffarpur district of Bihar. Its total length is 300 kms. (192 miles).
It is said that when the river goddess asked for a boon, विष्णु said he would always reside in her in the form of शालग्राम stones. The part of the river in Nepal near Muktinātha abounds in these stones, considered as emblems of विष्णु and extremely holy.

Gaṇeśa-caturthī
------------------------------------------
Gaṇeśa or गणपति, the elephant-faced god, is an extremely popular deity, not only with the masses but also with the classes. Being Vighneśvara—Lord of and destroyer of obstacles—he is eagerly sought by the classes. The masses try to propitiate him to fulfil their needs, since he is ‘Varada’ and ‘Siddhida,’ the giver of boons and success in undertakings. No venture can be started without worshipping him first. He is also the god of knowledge and wisdom as well as literature and fine-arts. Hence the supreme importance of the गणेश-चतुर्थी-vrata.
The पुराणस् are replete with his stories, that describe his origin or adventures, or that contain philosophical disquisitions delving into his symbology. Pundits have been battling over the years to solve the riddles concerning the origin or evolution of the enigmatic deity. We are however interested in harnessing his grace and powers for the benefit of the devotees by describing some relevant details concerning the vrata which has been so highly extolled in the Hindu religious works.
The main time for the performance of पूजा to गणेश on this sacred day is noon. A clay image, beautifully painted, is to be brought and installed on a suitable altar, and decorated. After the usual preliminary rites, प्राणप्रतिष्ठा (‘infusing life into the image’ or ‘invoking the presence of the deity into the image’) has to be done with appropriate mantras. This should be followed by worship with sixteen उपचारस् or modes of showing honour. Offering of दूर्वा (grass) tendrils and modaka (a kind of sweet supposed to be dear to गणेश), twenty-one in number, is a very important part of this पूजा. This may symbolically teach us that we have to offer in all humility (represented by the दूर्वा grass), all the good things of life that give us pleasure and happiness (represented by the modaka; ‘modaka’ literally means ‘that which gives us joy’). The number 21 may stand for the 21 items in our person viz., ज्ञानेन्द्रियस् or the five organs of perception, कर्मेन्द्रियस् or the five organs of action, the five prāṇas or vital airs, the five bhūtas or elements and the मिन्द्. Thus the पूजा can teach us total dedication and surrender at the feet of Lord गणेश, who is none other than the highest ब्रह्मन् or the Absolute in that form. The image has to be ceremonially immersed in water after the completion of the vrata.
In modern times, the image is kept and worshipped for 1½ days or 2 to 7 days or even up to Anantacaturdaśī (14th day of bright half of Bhādrapada) before immersing. It is taken in a procession for the immersion which is done in a well or a tank or a river or the sea.
There is a widespread popular belief that if one sees the मोओन् on the गणेश Caturthī day, he will be falsely charged with the commission of a theft or a similar crime. The story of Śrī कृष्ण being thus implicated in the theft of the famous gold-yielding gem (syamantaka) belonging to the Yādava chieftain Satrājit is cited as an example. (This story appears in the Mahābhārata as also in several पुराणस् such as Vāyu, Matsya, Viṣṇu and Bhāga-vata.) The problem has also been ‘solved’ by these works, by recommending to such inadvertent ‘offenders’ the recitation of a मन्त्र 1 जाम्बवान्. Don't cry, O tender child ! This syamantaka jewel belongs to you.'">2 over some water and drinking it.
One more गणेश Caturthī is mentioned in some पुराणस्, as falling on Māgha śukla caturthī . But it is not being observed now.

Gaṇapati
(‘lord of the groups [of deities]’)
------------------------------------------
Gaṇapati or गणेश, also known as विनायक, is perhaps, the most popular of the Hindu deities worshipped by all sections of the Hindus. No undertaking, whether sacred or secular, can get started without first honouring and worshipping him. This is understandable and highly desirable, since he is said to be the lord of obstacles (Vighneśvara or Vighnarāja). However, what is not understandable and certainly not very agreeable is his repulsive origin and grotesque form! Even for those who admire Lord शिव’s skill in the surgical art of head-transplantation, it becomes rather difficult to admire the end-product! Once we successfully manage to delve into the mysteries of this symbolism our repugnance will give rise to respect and respect to reverence and worship.
Notwithstanding the fact that the गणपति referred to in the famous Ṛgvedic mantras, ‘gaṇānāṁ tvā gaṇapatiṁ havā-mahe...’ (2.23.1) and ‘niṣu sīda gaṇapate...’ (10.112.9) and the गणपति we worship today are strangers to each other, all unbiased scholars agree that the seeds of the गणपति concept are already there in the Ṛgveda itself. In the subsequent centuries, this concept has passed through the mills of the epics and the पुराणस् to produce the गणपति as we know him today. In any community, the development of the concept of God and the modes of his worship are as much the products of geographical, historical and cultural factors as of mystic experience and spiritual realizations of the highly evolved persons. It is quite reasonable to suppose that the ‘Gaṇapati-ब्रह्मणस्पति’ of the Ṛgveda gradually got metamorphosed into the deity, ‘Gajavadana-गणेश-Vighneśvara.’
The Ṛgvedic deity ‘Gaṇapati-Brahma-ṇaspati’—also called बृहस्पति and Vācaspati—manifests himself through a vast mass of light. He is golden-red in colour. The battle axe is an important weapon of his. Without his grace no religious rite can succeed. He is always in the company of a group (gaṇa = a group) of singers and dancers. He vanquishes the enemies of gods, protects the devoted votaries and shows them the right way of life.
Another class of Ṛgvedic deities, known as the Maruts or मरुद्गण, described as the children of रुद्र, also have similar characteristics. In addition, they can be malevolent towards those who antagonise them and can cause destruction like the wild elephants. They can put obstacles in the path of men if displeased and remove them when pleased. They are independent, not subject to any one’s sovereignty (Arājana = विनायक).
A perusal of these two descriptions will perforce lead us to the obvious conclusion that गणपति is the metamorphosed form of the बृहस्पति-मरुद्गण deities. There is nothing strange in this, especially if we can recognize the transformations that have taken place among the various Vedic deities, as they were gradually absorbed among the gods of the later Hindu pantheon. The once all-important and all-powerful इन्द्र was demoted to the rank of a minor deity ruling over one of the quarters. His lieutenant विष्णु was elevated to the central place in the Trinity. रुद्र, the terrible, became शिव the auspicious. Many other deities like द्यौस्, अर्यमन् and पूषन् were quietly despatched into oblivion!
Despite the fact that गणपति is a highly venerated and all-important deity, his ‘head’ has often been a mystery for others. No doubt, our पुराणस् have easily ‘solved’ this problem, each in its own way. But this has satisfied neither the layman nor the scholar.
It will be extremely interesting to bring together, though in brief, all the stories about the origin of this wondrous deity:
At the request of the gods who wanted a deity capable of removing all obstacles from their path of action and fulfilment, शिव himself was born of the womb of पार्वती as Gajānana.
Once पार्वती, just for fun, prepared an image of a child with an elephant’s head, out of the unguents smeared over her body and threw it into the river गङ्गा. It came to life. Both गङ्गा, the guardian deity of the river and पार्वती, addressed the boy as their child. Hence he is known as Dvaimātura, ‘one who has two mothers’.
Pārvatī prepared the image of a child out of the scurf from her body, endowed him with life and ordered him to stand guard before her होउसे. When शिव wanted to enter the होउसे he was rudely prevented by this new gatekeeper. शिव became ‘Rudra’ and got him beheaded. Seeing that पार्वती was inconsolable owing to this tragedy that befell her ‘son’ and not finding the head of the body anywhere—meanwhile one of the goblins of शिव had gourmandized it!—he got an elephant’s head, grafted it on to the body of the boy and gave him life. To make amends for his ‘mistake,’ शिव appointed this new-found son as the head of all his retinues, who thus became ‘Gaṇapati’.
He sprang from शिव’s countenance which represents the principle of ether (ākāśatattva). His captivating splendour made पार्वती react angrily and curse him, resulting in his uncouth form!
Gaṇeśa was originally कृष्ण himself in the human form. When शनि, the malevolent planet spirit gazed at him, his head got separated and flew to गोलोक, the world of कृष्ण. The head of an elephant was subsequently grafted on the body of the child.
Equally interesting are the other myths about his adventures: He lost one of his tusks in a fight with परशुराम, which he successfully used as a stylus to write the epic Mahābhārata dictated by the sage व्यास. He tactfully won the race against his brother स्कन्द by circumambulating his parents and declaring that it was equivalent to going round the worlds. He thus won the hands of two damsels ऋद्धि and Siddhi. He cursed the मोओन् to wax and wane, since the latter derisively laughed at him when he was trying to refill his burst belly with the sweets that had spilled out. He vanquished the demon Vighnāsura and successfully brought him under his subjugation.
There is no gainsaying the possibilities of man developing the concept of God and faith in him as a result of his experiences through the various vicissitudes of life which prove his helplessness. He often disposes, what he proposes. Such a God must needs be all powerful. If he is pleased, all the obstacles in our path will be removed. If displeased, He may thwart our efforts and make them infructuous. Hence the paramount need to appease Him and please Him.
What could be the form of this almighty God? For a simple aboriginal living in a group (= गण) near a forest or a mountain, the mighty elephant might have provided the clue. This might have led to the worship of an elephant-like God. He being the pati (= Lord) of the गण (clan or group) might have obtained the name गणपति. As the group became more refined and cultured, this Elephant God might have been transformed into the present form.
However plausible or attractive this hypothesis may be, it is at best a guesswork, if not an invention! Since गणपति had gained de facto recognition in the hearts of millions of votaries, over several centuries, the पुराणस् rightly struggled to make it de jure! True, they have given very confusing accounts. Nevertheless they have succeeded in fusing together the votaries by giving them a scriptural or authoritative base. There is certainly no contradiction or confusion in the accounts as far as the worship and its results are concerned.
It is a favourite pastime of some Western scholars and their Indian counter-parts to ‘discover’ a Draviḍian base for many interesting developments in our cultural and religious life and then to ‘unearth’ the further fact of the white-skinned Āryan ‘conquerors’ graciously and condescendingly absorbing these, tactfully elevating the same to ‘higher’ levels all the while. This has naturally led to a vigorous reaction and these ‘reactionaries’ go the whole hog to ‘prove’ it the other way round! When our गणपति is caught in the web of such controversies one may be driven to the ridiculous conclusion that he is not an Āryan deity at all, but, most probably, imported from Mongolia! It is therefore better to play safe, rescue our deity from embarrassing situations and get the best out of him for our spiritual life.
The most commonly accepted form of गणपति depicts him as red in colour and in a human body with an elephant’s head. Out of the two tusks, one is broken. He has four arms. Two of the arms hold the पाश (noose) and aṅkuśa (goad). The other two are held in the abhaya and varada mudrās. The belly is of generous proportions and is decorated with a snake-belt. There is also a यज्ञोपवीत (sacred brahminical thread), either of thread or of serpent. He may be seated in पद्मासन (lotus-posture). When the belly does not permit this, the right leg may be shown bent and resting on the seat.
Apart from beautiful robes and ornaments, he wears a lovely carved crown.
The trunk may be turned to the left or to the right.
He is normally seen helping himself to liberal quantities of modaka (a kind of sweet).
A mouse, of ridiculously small proportions, is seen near him, nibbling at his share of the sweets, hoping perhaps, to gain enough strength to carry his master!
A third eye may sometimes be added on the forehead, in the centre of the eyebrows. The number of heads may be raised to five. The arms may vary from two to ten. Lotus, pomegranate, water-vessel, battle-axe, lute, broken tusk, sugarcane, ears of paddy, bow and arrow, thunderbolt, rosary, book—these are some of the other objects shown in the hands. His Śaktis are often shown with him as sitting on his lap. Sometimes two Śaktis, ऋद्धि बुद्धि.">1 and Siddhi, are also shown.
Let us now make an attempt at unravelling this symbology.
‘Gaṇa’ means category. Everything that we perceive through our senses or grasp through our मिन्द् can be expressed in terms of kind, of category. The principle from which all such categories have manifested themselves is गणपति, the Lord of categories. In effect, it means the origin of the whole च्रेअतिओन्, God himself.
A common Sanskrit word to denote the elephant is ‘Gaja’. Hence the name Gajānana or Gajamukha (‘elephant-faced’) for गणपति. But the word ‘Gaja’ has a much deeper connotation. ‘Ga’ indicates ‘gati’, the final goal towards which the entire च्रेअतिओन् is moving, whether knowingly or unknowingly; ‘ja’ stands for ‘janma’, birth or origin. Hence ‘Gaja’ signifies God from whom the worlds have come out and towards whom they are progressing, to be ultimately dissolved in him. The elephant head is thus purely symbolical and points to this truth. Another factor we observe in च्रेअतिओन् is its two-fold manifestation as the microcosm (sūkṣmāṇḍa) and the macrocosm (brahmāṇḍa). Each is a replica of the other. They are one in two and two in one. The elephant head stands for the macrocosm and the human body for the microcosm. The two form one unit. Since the macrocosm is the goal of the microcosm, the elephant part has been given greater prominence by making it the head.
Perhaps, the boldest statement concerning philosophical truths ever made is contained in that pithy saying of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (6.8.7): ‘tat-tvam-asi’, ‘That thou art’. It simply means: ‘You, the apparently limited individual, are, in essence, the Cosmic Truth, the Absolute.’ The elephant-human form of गणपति is the iconographical representation of this great Vedāntic dictum. The elephant stands for the cosmic whereas the human stands for the individual. The single image reflects their identity.
Among the various myths that deal with गणपति’s origin, the one that attributes it to the scurf or dirt taken out of her body by पार्वती seems to be the most widely known, and considered as odd and odious. It is therefore worthwhile to delve a little deeper into this mystery.
One of the epithets by which गणपति is well-known and worshipped is ‘Vighneśvara’ or ‘Vighnarāja’ (‘the Lord of obstacles’). He is the lord of all that obstructs or restricts, hinders or prevents. With the various grades and shades of the powers of obstruction under his control, he can create a हेल्ल् of trouble for us if he wants! In fact, according to the mythological accounts, the very purpose of his च्रेअतिओन् was to obstruct the progress in the path of perfection!
How does he do it? If he is not appeased by proper worship, all undertakings, whether sacred or secular, will meet with so many obstacles that they will simply peter out. This is to show that nothing can succeed without his grace. If he is pleased by worship and service, he will tempt his votaries with success and prosperity (siddhi and ऋद्धि) the very taste of which can gradually lead them away from the spiritual path. Why does he do it? To test them thoroughly before conferring upon them the greatest spiritual boon of मोक्ष. Being the master of all arts and sciences, and the repository of all knowledge, He can easily confer success or perfection in any of these. However, he is unwilling to give spiritual knowledge leading to the highest spiritual experience, lest it should appear easy of achievement in the eyes of men. Hence the severity of the test. The path of the good is fraught with innumerable obstacles, ‘śreyāṁsi bahuvighnāni.’ Only the very best of heroes, who can brave the roughest of weathers, deserve to be blessed with it. Human beings by nature are inclined towards the enjoyments of the flesh and intoxications of power and pelf. It is only one in a million that turns towards God. Among many such souls, very few survive the struggles and reach the goal. (vide Gītā 7.3)
When compared to the highest spiritual wisdom, which alone is really worth striving for, even ऋद्धि and siddhi (success and prosperity) are like impurities, मल, as it were. Since गणपति’s consorts are ऋद्धि and Siddhi (personifications of the powers of success and prosperity), he, their spouse, has been described as created out of पार्वती’s bodily scurf.
Again the word ‘mala’ need not have any odium about it. If शिव represents Paramapuruṣa, the Supreme Person, पार्वती stands for Paramā प्रकृति, Nature Supreme, considered as his power, inseparable from him. She is, in the language of philosophy, Māyāprakṛti, comprising the three guṇas—sattva, रजस् and तमस्. सत्त्व is stated to be pure and, as compared to it, रजस् and तमस् are said to be ‘impure’. Since च्रेअतिओन् is impossible out of pure सत्त्व, even as pure gold does not lend itself to be shaped into ornaments unless mixed with baser metals, it has got to be mixed with रजस् and तमस् to effect it. This seems to be the import of the story of the ‘impure’ substances being used by मोथेर् पार्वती to shape गणपति.
Let us now try to interpret the other factors involved in the symbology of this god. His ears are large, large enough to listen to the supplications of everyone, but, like the winnowing basket, are capable of sifting what is good for the supplicant from what is not. Out of the two tusks, the one that is whole stands for the Truth, the One without a second. The broken tusk, which is imperfect, stands for the manifest world, which appears to be imperfect because of the inherent incongruities. However, the manifest universe and the unmanifest unity are both attributes of the same Absolute. The bent trunk is a representation of ओङ्कार or प्रणव which being the symbol of ब्रह्मन्, the Absolute, is declaring as it were that गणपति is ब्रह्मन् Itself. His large belly indicates that all the created worlds are contained in him.
The पाश (noose) stands for राग (attachment), and the aṅkuśa (goad) for krodha (anger). Like the noose, attachment binds us. Anger hurts us like the goad. If God is displeased with us, our attachments and anger will increase, making us miserable. The only way of escaping from the tyranny of these is to take refuge in God. Or it can mean that it is far safer for us to surrender our attachment and anger to him. When they are in his hands, we are safe!
How we wish that Lord गणपति had chosen a big bandicoot as his mount. The fact, however, is otherwise and that privilege has been conferred on a small mouse! The word mūṣaka (= mouse) is derived from the root ‘muṣ’ which means ‘to steal’. A mouse stealthily enters into things and destroys them from within. Similarly egoism enters unnoticed, into our minds and quietly destroys all our undertakings. Only when it is controlled by divine wisdom, it can be harnessed to useful channels. Or, the mouse that steals, can represent love that steals the human hearts. As long as human love is kept at the low level, it can create havoc. Once it is directed towards the Divine, it elevates us. The mouse that is wont to see the inside of all things can stand for the incisive intellect. Since गणपति is the lord of the intellect, it is but meet that he has chosen it as his vehicle.
Icons of Gaṇapati
There are several varieties of गणपति icons available in our temples and archaeological monuments. Whether the number is 71, 50, 31 or 21, it is certain that there are several aspects of this deity. Only a few of them can be dealt with here.
‘Bālagaṇapati’ and ‘Taruṇagaṇapati’ images depict him as a child and a young man, respectively. ‘Vināyaka’ is shown with four arms holding the broken tusk, goad, noose and rosary. He holds the sweet modaka in his trunk. He may be standing or seated. ‘Herambagaṇapati’ has five heads, ten hands, three eyes in each face and rides on a lion. ‘Vīravighneśa’ exhibits the martial spirit with several weapons held in his ten hands. ‘Śaktigaṇapati,’ several varieties of which are described in the तन्त्रस्, is shown with his शक्ति, called variously as लक्ष्मी, ऋद्धि, Siddhi, Puṣṭi and so on. Worship of this aspect is said to confer special powers or grant the desired fruits quickly.
One of the varieties of this ‘Śakti-गणपति’ is called ‘Ucchiṣṭagaṇapati,’ the गणपति associated with unclean things whose worship belongs to वामाचार (‘the left-handed path,’ i.e., the heterodox and unclean path) and said to give quick results. There is nothing to dread or recoil in this concept. Dirty things are as much a part of nature as clean things, but, do not scavengers and doctors handle them in a hygienic way and serve the people? Are not all people obliged to be scavengers in varying degrees? Why not do it reli-giously, as an act of service and worship? Nature converts clean things into unclean things and vice versa. Making गणपति preside over it and handle dirt scientifically and religiously can also be a spiritual discipline. This seems to be the philosophy behind this concept.
‘Nṛttagaṇapati’ is a beautiful image showing him as dancing. It seems once ब्रह्मा met गणपति and bowed down to him with great devotion and reverence. Being pleased with this, गणपति started dancing gracefully. That is why गणपति is declared to be the master of the arts of मुसिच् and dancing.
‘Varasiddhi विनायक’ is the aspect worshipped during the famous गणेश Caturthī festival. He is said to be a celibate.
Gaṇapati is sometimes depicted as a शक्ति (female deity) under the names of Gaṇeśānī, Vināyakī, Śūrpakarṇī, Lamba-mekhalā and so on.
Gaṇapati is worshipped not only in images but also in liṅgas, śālagrāmas, yantras (geometrical diagrams) and kalaśas (pots of water). गणपति śāla-grāmas however, are very rare. The स्वस्तिक is also accepted as a graphic symbol of गणपति.
Temples and shrines dedicated to गणपति are very numerous. They are spread all over the country. He appears in the campuses of temples of most other deities also.

gaṇa
(‘group’)
------------------------------------------
This word has been used in several senses, often as a technical term also. The most general meaning is ‘an assemblage or a group.’
In the पुराणस् the word is widely used to indicate the pramatha-गण, the group of demi-gods, the associates of शिव. गणपति or गणेश, the famous and popular deity of the Hindu pantheon, is their leader.
Sometimes, the पुराणस् also mention ‘gaṇadevatās,’ special classes of deities. They are 422 in number distributed among nine classes as follows: Ādityas (12), विश्वेदेवस् (10), वसुस् (8), Tuṣitas (36), Ābhāsvaras (64), Anilas (49), Mahārājikas (220), Sādhyas (12) and Rudras (11).
In the military science it indicates one of the four formations of an armed force the proportion of the four aṅgas or limbs being as follows—
27 elephants: 27 chariots: 81 horses: 135 foot-soldiers.
The nakṣatras or groups of lunar mansions are also divided into gaṇas such as Devagaṇa, (Aśvinī, Mṛgaśiras etc.), Naragaṇa (Bharaṇī, आर्द्रा etc.) and Rākṣasa-गण (Kṛttikā, Citrā etc.). This grouping helps the astrologers to match the horoscopes of the boy and the girl for मर्रिअगे.
In Sanskrit prosody, eight gaṇas, each comprising three syllables, are recognised. By the permutation and combination of these, several metres are obtained. For instance, the ‘ya-गण’ has three syllables—one laghu (short) and two gurus (long). Similarly the other gaṇas like ma-गण, ta-गण, ra-गण and so on, are also defined.
The word is also used in Sanskrit grammar to indicate the groups of certain padas or words (like gaura and utsa) as also dhātus or verbal roots (like bhū-ādi, ad-ādi and so on). They have their own utility in the various grammatical processes.
‘Gaṇa’ is also a term signifying a certain type of courts administering the laws of Hindu republics.
